claim: Bone-resorbing osteoclasts (OCLs) were recently identified as innate immune cells activating T cells toward tolerance or inflammation.
source: Bone-resorbing osteoclasts (OCLs) were recently identified as innate immune cells activating T cells toward tolerance or inflammation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Buchwald et al., 2012; Ibáñez et al., 2016; Kiesel et al., 2009; Li et al., 2010) in the Introduction section.

claim: Pathological bone destruction relies on the presence of inflammatory OCLs (i-OCLs), part of which express Cx3cr1.
source: Thus, pathological bone destruction not only relies on increased osteoclast differentiation, but also on the presence of inflammatory OCLs (i-OCLs), part of which express Cx3cr1.
evidence: This is a central claim of the study, supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Cx3cr1+ and Cx3cr1neg i-OCLs differ considerably in transcriptional and functional aspects.
source: We showed that Cx3cr1+ and Cx3cr1neg i-OCLs differ considerably in transcriptional and functional aspects.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data and functional assays presented in Figures 3-6.

claim: Cx3cr1neg i-OCLs have a high ability to resorb bone and activate inflammatory CD4+ T cells.
source: Cx3cr1neg i-OCLs have a high ability to resorb bone and activate inflammatory CD4+ T cells.
evidence: This is supported by resorption assays (Figure 4E-F) and T cell activation assays (Figure 5G).

claim: Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs resorb less bone than Cx3cr1neg i-OCLs.
source: Although Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs are associated with inflammation, they resorb less and have in vitro an immune-suppressive effect on Cx3cr1neg i-OCLs, mediated by PD-L1.
evidence: This is supported by resorption assays shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs have an immune-suppressive effect on Cx3cr1neg i-OCLs mediated by PD-L1.
source: Although Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs are associated with inflammation, they resorb less and have in vitro an immune-suppressive effect on Cx3cr1neg i-OCLs, mediated by PD-L1.
evidence: This is supported by immunosuppression assays (Figure 6E) and anti-PD-1 blocking experiments (Figure 6C).

claim: Cx3cr1 deficiency protects against inflammatory bone loss in ovariectomized mice.
source: Cx3cr1 deficiency protects against inflammatory bone loss in osteoporosis
evidence: This is supported by micro-CT analysis showing higher BV/TV and trabecular number in Cx3cr1-deficient OVX mice (Figure 1B-C).

claim: After ovariectomy, Cx3cr1-deficient mice displayed moderate but significant higher BV/TV and trabecular number and lower trabecular separation than WT Cx3cr1GFP/+ mice.
source: Micro-CT analysis revealed that after ovariectomy, Cx3cr1-deficient mice displayed moderate but significant higher BV/TV and trabecular number and lower trabecular separation than WT Cx3cr1GFP/+ mice (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This is directly supported by micro-CT data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Cx3cr1-deficient OVX mice had less TRAcP+ OCLs compared to OVX WT Cx3cr1GFP/+ mice.
source: They also had less TRAcP+ OCLs compared to OVX WT Cx3cr1GFP/+ mice (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by TRAcP staining shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Cx3cr1+ OCLs increased after ovariectomy in WT OVX mice.
source: We previously showed that Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs increased in inflammatory colitis associated with bone destruction (Ibáñez et al., 2016) and we confirmed here that they also increased after ovariectomy in WT OVX mice (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Both DCs and Ly6Chi MNs increased in the BM of OVX Cx3cr1GFP/+ but not Cx3cr1GFP/GFP mice.
source: FACS analysis in OVX mice revealed that both DCs and Ly6Chi MNs increased in the BM of OVX Cx3cr1GFP/+ but not Cx3cr1GFP/GFP mice (Figure 1E–F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: The reduced bone loss observed in Cx3cr1-deficient Cx3cr1GFP/GFP mice is, at least partly, related to a decrease in BM progenitors of Cx3cr1+ OCLs, namely DCs and Ly6Chi MNs.
source: These results suggest that the reduced bone loss observed in Cx3cr1-deficient Cx3cr1GFP/GFP mice is, at least partly, related to a decrease in BM progenitors of Cx3cr1+ OCLs, namely DCs and Ly6Chi MNs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing reduced DCs and Ly6Chi MNs in Cx3cr1-deficient mice (Figure 1E-F).

claim: About 35% of OCLs derived from blood Ly6Chi MNs expressed GFP indicating that Ly6Chi MNs are progenitors of Cx3cr1+ OCLs.
source: About 35% of the resulting OCLs expressed GFP indicating that Ly6Chi MNs are also progenitors of Cx3cr1+ OCLs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Cx3cr1 deficiency does not alter immune and bone resorption function of Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs.
source: Cx3cr1 deficiency does not alter immune and bone resorption function of Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs
evidence: This is supported by functional assays comparing GFP+ i-OCLs from Cx3cr1GFP/GFP and Cx3cr1GFP/+ mice (Figure 2C-G).

claim: No differences were detected between GFP+ i-OCLs from Cx3cr1-deficient Cx3cr1GFP/+ and WT Cx3cr1GFP/GFP mice except for their Cx3cr1 expression.
source: Except for their Cx3cr1 expression, no differences were detected between GFP+ i-OCLs from Cx3cr1-deficient Cx3cr1GFP/+ and WT Cx3cr1GFP/GFP mice suggesting that Cx3cr1 deficiency did not change the identity of i-OCLs (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: GFP+ i-OCLs from Cx3cr1-deficient Cx3cr1GFP/+ and WT Cx3cr1GFP/GFP mice had equivalent resorption activity.
source: Similarly, functional in vitro assays revealed that regardless if they derived from Cx3cr1-deficient Cx3cr1GFP/+ or WT Cx3cr1GFP/GFP mice, GFP+ i-OCLs had equivalent resorption activity, antigen-presentation capacity or expression of MHC-II and co-stimulatory molecules (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is supported by resorption assays shown in Figure 2C.

claim: GFP+ i-OCLs from Cx3cr1-deficient Cx3cr1GFP/+ and WT Cx3cr1GFP/GFP mice had equivalent antigen-presentation capacity.
source: Similarly, functional in vitro assays revealed that regardless if they derived from Cx3cr1-deficient Cx3cr1GFP/+ or WT Cx3cr1GFP/GFP mice, GFP+ i-OCLs had equivalent resorption activity, antigen-presentation capacity or expression of MHC-II and co-stimulatory molecules (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is supported by OVA uptake assays shown in Figure 2D.

claim: No differences between GFP+ i-OCLs from Cx3cr1GFP/GFP versus Cx3cr1GFP/+ mice were found in their T cell activation and polarization capacity.
source: No differences between GFP+ i-OCLs from Cx3cr1GFP/GFP versus Cx3cr1GFP/+ mice were found in their T cell activation and polarization capacity (Figure 2F–G).
evidence: This is supported by T cell proliferation and cytokine production assays shown in Figure 2F-G.

claim: The function of the Cx3xr1 protein per se is not essential for the resorption and immune function of mature Cx3cr1-expressing i-OCLs.
source: Thus, our results indicate that the function of the Cx3xr1 protein per se is not essential for the resorption and immune function of mature Cx3cr1-expressing i-OCLs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of functional differences between Cx3cr1-deficient and WT Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs (Figure 2C-G).

claim: A total of 1771 genes were significantly differentially expressed between Cx3cr1+ and Cx3cr1neg i-OCLs.
source: A total of 1771 genes were significantly differentially expressed (adj.pVal <0.05, Log2FC ≥ 1) between the 2 populations.
evidence: This is directly stated based on RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Principal Component Analysis revealed that Cx3cr1+ (GFP+) and Cx3cr1neg (GFPneg) i-OCLs were clustered into 2 distinct populations.
source: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) of all detectable genes revealed that Cx3cr1+ (GFP+) and Cx3cr1neg (GFPneg) i-OCLs were clustered into 2 distinct populations (Figure 3B), which was reinforced by volcano plot and hierarchical clustering analysis of the top 107 significantly differently expressed genes (adj.pVal <0.05 and Log2FC ≥ 1) (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Genes interacting with the Cx3cr1 functional pathway were differentially expressed between Cx3cr1+ and Cx3cr1neg i-OCLs.
source: In addition to Cx3cr1, genes interacting with its functional pathway were also differentially expressed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Nr1d1, a negative regulator of Cx3cr1, was reduced in Cx3cr1+ versus Cx3cr1neg i-OCLs.
source: In particular, Nr1d1, a negative regulator of Cx3cr1 (Song et al., 2018) was reduced whereas Tlr4 that mediates Cx3cr1 upregulation by LPS (Panek et al., 2015) was increased in Cx3cr1+ versus Cx3cr1neg i-OCLs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and cited literature.

claim: Tlr4 that mediates Cx3cr1 upregulation by LPS was increased in Cx3cr1+ versus Cx3cr1neg i-OCLs.
source: In particular, Nr1d1, a negative regulator of Cx3cr1 (Song et al., 2018) was reduced whereas Tlr4 that mediates Cx3cr1 upregulation by LPS (Panek et al., 2015) was increased in Cx3cr1+ versus Cx3cr1neg i-OCLs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and cited literature.

claim: Cx3cr1+ OCLs could be generated from either Cx3cr1+ or Cx3cr1neg BM-derived DCs.
source: This was further confirmed by showing that Cx3cr1+ OCLs could be generated from either Cx3cr1+ or Cx3cr1neg BM-derived DCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The expression of Cx3cr1 in i-OCLs is not only inherited from their progenitors but may be acquired through a dynamic up-regulation during the differentiation of a subset of i-OCLs.
source: Thus, the expression of Cx3cr1 in i-OCLs is not only inherited from their progenitors but may be acquired through a dynamic up-regulation during the differentiation of a subset of i-OCLs having a specific function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Cx3cr1+ OCLs can arise from Cx3cr1neg progenitors (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Cx3cr1neg i-OCLs expressed higher levels of genes responsible for bone resorption than Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs.
source: Transcriptomic profiling revealed that Cx3cr1neg i-OCLs expressed higher levels of genes responsible for bone resorption (Figure 4A), which was confirmed by RT-qPCR (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 4A) and RT-qPCR validation (Figure 4B).

claim: Both Cx3cr1neg and Cx3cr1+ i-OCL subsets differed from BM-derived macrophages as they did not express CD68 and CD169.
source: Our results revealed that both Cx3cr1neg and Cx3cr1+ i-OCL subsets differed from BM-derived macrophages as they did not express CD68 and CD169 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: Both Cx3cr1neg and Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs subsets shared the main characteristics of OCLs, e.g. TRAcP expression and resorption activity.
source: Moreover, the 2 i-OCLs subsets shared the main characteristics of OCLs, e.g. TRAcP expression and resorption activity (Figure 4C–F) while BM-macrophages did not express TRAcP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by TRAcP staining (Figure 4C-D) and resorption assays (Figure 4E-F).

claim: Cx3cr1neg i-OCLs showed a higher matrix dissolution activity compared to Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs when seeded at the same cell concentration.
source: However, when sorted mature Cx3cr1neg and Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs were seeded at the same cell concentration, Cx3cr1neg i-OCLs showed a higher matrix dissolution activity compared to Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: This is supported by resorption assays shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: Cx3cr1neg and Cx3cr1+ subsets correspond to 2 subsets of bona fide OCLs that differ in their resorption activity.
source: These results demonstrate that Cx3cr1neg and Cx3cr1+ subsets correspond to 2 subsets of bona fide OCLs that differ in their resorption activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing both subsets express OCL markers but have different resorption capacities (Figure 4).

claim: RNA-seq data revealed significant differences in genes involved in antigen-processing and presentation between Cx3cr1+ and Cx3cr1neg i-OCLs.
source: Besides these differences in bone resorption, RNA-seq data revealed significant differences in genes involved in antigen-processing and presentation (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Both Cx3cr1+ and Cx3cr1neg i-OCL subsets engulfed OVA, but this capacity was significantly decreased in Cx3cr1neg i-OCLs.
source: Further in vitro analysis confirmed that whereas both i-OCL subsets engulfed OVA, this capacity was significantly decreased in Cx3cr1neg i-OCLs (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This is supported by OVA uptake assays shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: MHC-II molecules were more expressed in Cx3cr1neg than Cx3cr1pos i-OCLs.
source: In line with the RNA-seq data, FACS analysis confirmed that MHC-II molecules were more expressed in Cx3cr1neg than Cx3cr1pos i-OCLs (Figure 5D), while no significant differences were observed in the expression of CD80 and CD86 (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: No significant differences were observed in the expression of CD80 and CD86 between Cx3cr1neg and Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs.
source: In line with the RNA-seq data, FACS analysis confirmed that MHC-II molecules were more expressed in Cx3cr1neg than Cx3cr1pos i-OCLs (Figure 5D), while no significant differences were observed in the expression of CD80 and CD86 (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: Cx3cr1neg i-OCLs showed higher capacity to induce T cell proliferation than Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs.
source: Moreover, Cx3cr1neg i-OCLs showed higher capacity to induce T cell proliferation than Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by T cell proliferation assays shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Both Cx3cr1+ and Cx3cr1neg i-OCL subsets were able to induce TNFα and IFNγ-producing CD4+ T cells but not FoxP3+CD4+ regulatory T (Treg) cells.
source: Nevertheless, both i-OCL subsets were able to induce TNFα and IFNγ-producing CD4+ T cells but not FoxP3+CD4+ regulatory T (Treg) cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), in accordance with the previously described immune properties of i-OCLs (Ibáñez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by intracellular cytokine staining shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and cited literature.

claim: Both i-OCL subsets expressed inflammation-associated genes in line with their capacity to induce TNFα and IFNγ-producing CD4+ T cells.
source: RNA-seq data also revealed that both i-OCLs subsets expressed inflammation-associated genes in line with their capacity to induce TNFα and IFNγ-producing CD4+ T cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs had significant higher expression of immunosuppressive genes than Cx3cr1neg i-OCLs.
source: However, Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs had significant higher expression of immunosuppressive genes (Figure 6A) that could contribute to their lower inflammatory potential.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: RT-qPCR confirmed higher expression of CD274 (PD-L1), Lgals9 (Galectin-9) and Tnfrsf14 (HEVM) in Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs.
source: Further RT-qPCR of the immunosuppressive genes CD274 (PD-L1), Lgals9 (Galectin-9) and Tnfrsf14 (HEVM) confirmed these findings (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Blocking the PD-L1/PD-1 axis with an anti-PD-1 antibody increased the capacity of Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs to induce T cell proliferation.
source: Interestingly, blocking the PD-L1/PD-1 axis with an anti-PD-1 antibody in co-cultures of Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs and CD4+ T cells increased the capacity of Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs to induce T cell proliferation (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by T cell proliferation assays with anti-PD-1 antibody shown in Figure 6C.

claim: PD-L1 plays a central role in the immunosuppressive potential of Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs.
source: These findings reveal that PD-L1 plays a central role in the immunosuppressive potential of Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anti-PD-1 blocking experiment (Figure 6C).

claim: Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs could have an immunosuppressive effect on Cx3cr1neg i-OCLs.
source: They also suggest that Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs could have an immunosuppressive effect on Cx3cr1neg i-OCLs.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the high expression of immunosuppressive molecules in Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs.

claim: The addition of Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs dramatically decreased CD4+ T cell proliferation induced by Cx3cr1neg i-OCLs.
source: Cx3cr1neg i-OCLs alone (ratio 1:0) highly stimulated CD4+ T cell proliferation, which was dramatically decreased by the addition of Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs (ratio 1:2; Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by immunosuppression assays shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs are able to control the inflammatory activity of Cx3cr1neg i-OCLs in vitro.
source: These data demonstrate that Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs are able to control the inflammatory activity of Cx3cr1neg i-OCLs in vitro, suggesting the existence of a novel mechanism of interaction between OCLs in inflammatory conditions that remains to be addressed in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the immunosuppression assay data (Figure 6E).

claim: OCLs are long-lived multinucleated cells arising from bone marrow (BM) progenitors.
source: OCLs are long-lived multinucleated cells arising from bone marrow (BM) progenitors (Arai et al., 1999; Jacome-Galarza et al., 2013; Jacome-Galarza et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In inflammation, OCLs also arise from inflammatory Ly6Chi monocytes (MNs).
source: However, in inflammation, they also arise from inflammatory Ly6Chi monocytes (MNs) (Ammari et al., 2018; Seeling et al., 2013) and dendritic cells (DCs) including in vivo (Wakkach et al., 2008; Ibáñez et al., 2016; Mansour et al., 2012; Rivollier et al., 2004; Madel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In inflammation, OCLs also arise from dendritic cells (DCs) including in vivo.
source: However, in inflammation, they also arise from inflammatory Ly6Chi monocytes (MNs) (Ammari et al., 2018; Seeling et al., 2013) and dendritic cells (DCs) including in vivo (Wakkach et al., 2008; Ibáñez et al., 2016; Mansour et al., 2012; Rivollier et al., 2004; Madel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: OCLs permanently fuse with MNs and undergo fission to maintain their nuclei number.
source: Furthermore, OCLs permanently fuse with MNs and undergo fission to maintain their nuclei number (Jacome-Galarza et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In steady state or when derived from BM MNs of healthy mice, OCLs activate regulatory CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (tolerogenic-OCLs/t OCLs).
source: We and others showed that depending on their origin and environment, OCLs induce different T cell responses. In steady state or when derived from BM MNs of healthy mice, OCLs activate regulatory CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (tolerogenic-OCLs/t OCLs) (Ibáñez et al., 2016; Kiesel et al., 2009), whereas when derived from DCs or during inflammation, they induce TNFα-producing CD4+ T cells (inflammatory-OCLs/i-OCLs) (Ibáñez et al., 2016; Madel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: When derived from DCs or during inflammation, OCLs induce TNFα-producing CD4+ T cells (inflammatory-OCLs/i-OCLs).
source: We and others showed that depending on their origin and environment, OCLs induce different T cell responses. In steady state or when derived from BM MNs of healthy mice, OCLs activate regulatory CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (tolerogenic-OCLs/t OCLs) (Ibáñez et al., 2016; Kiesel et al., 2009), whereas when derived from DCs or during inflammation, they induce TNFα-producing CD4+ T cells (inflammatory-OCLs/i-OCLs) (Ibáñez et al., 2016; Madel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: According to their origin and environment, OCLs are heterogeneous and initiate different immune responses.
source: Thus, according to their origin and environment, OCLs are heterogeneous and initiate different immune responses.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cited literature and the authors' previous work.

claim: Cx3cr1 was identified as a marker identifying i-OCLs.
source: Recently, we identified the fractalkine receptor Cx3cr1 as a marker identifying i-OCLs (Ibáñez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: Cx3cr1 is expressed by OCL precursors and mediates their BM recruitment by Cx3cl1-producing endothelial cells and osteoblasts.
source: Cx3cr1 is expressed by OCL precursors and mediates their BM recruitment by Cx3cl1-producing endothelial cells and osteoblasts (Han et al., 2014; Hasegawa et al., 2019; Koizumi et al., 2009; Matsuura et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: During osteoclastogenesis, the level of expression of Cx3cr1 decreases and is very low in t-OCLs.
source: During osteoclastogenesis, the level of expression of Cx3cr1 decreases and is very low in t-OCLs (Hoshino et al., 2013; Koizumi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In inflammatory conditions, Cx3cr1 remains expressed in about 25% of i-OCLs.
source: However, in inflammatory conditions, Cx3cr1 remains expressed in about 25% of i-OCLs (Ibáñez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: Cx3cr1 is involved in the development and progression of chronic inflammatory diseases, such as colitis and arthritis.
source: Cx3cr1 is involved in the development and progression of chronic inflammatory diseases, such as colitis and arthritis (Kotani et al., 2013; Rossini et al., 2014; Tarrant et al., 2012) while Cx3cr1 deficiency reduces the severity of these diseases (Niess and Adler, 2010; Rossini et al., 2014; Tarrant et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cx3cr1 deficiency reduces the severity of chronic inflammatory diseases such as colitis and arthritis.
source: Cx3cr1 is involved in the development and progression of chronic inflammatory diseases, such as colitis and arthritis (Kotani et al., 2013; Rossini et al., 2014; Tarrant et al., 2012) while Cx3cr1 deficiency reduces the severity of these diseases (Niess and Adler, 2010; Rossini et al., 2014; Tarrant et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The OVX model is driven by TNFα and RANK-L-producing CD4+ T cells.
source: As in inflammatory bowel disease, this model is driven by TNFα and RANK-L-producing CD4+ T cells leading to the development of Cx3cr1+ OCLs (Cenci et al., 2000; Ibáñez et al., 2016; Weitzmann and Pacifici, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Fractalkine/Cx3cl1 increases in OVX mice and osteoporotic patients and correlates with disease severity.
source: Its ligand (Fractalkine/Cx3cl1) increases in OVX mice and osteoporotic patients and correlates with disease severity (Chen et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Fractalkine-producing mesenchymal cells attract OCL precursors and support their differentiation.
source: Fractalkine-producing mesenchymal cells attract OCL precursors and support their differentiation (Goto et al., 2016; Matsuura et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The Cx3cr1/Cx3cl1 axis is essential for the increased BM recruitment and differentiation of i-OCL progenitors observed in OVX mice.
source: Overall, our results demonstrate that the Cx3cr1/Cx3cl1 axis is essential for the increased BM recruitment and differentiation of i-OCL progenitors observed in OVX mice but that the Cx3cr1 protein per se is not involved in the resorption and immune function of fully mature i-OCLs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the in vivo and in vitro data presented in the study.

claim: The Cx3cr1 protein per se is not involved in the resorption and immune function of fully mature i-OCLs.
source: Overall, our results demonstrate that the Cx3cr1/Cx3cl1 axis is essential for the increased BM recruitment and differentiation of i-OCL progenitors observed in OVX mice but that the Cx3cr1 protein per se is not involved in the resorption and immune function of fully mature i-OCLs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of Cx3cr1-deficient and WT Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs (Figure 2).

claim: Cx3cr1+ OCLs are induced by inflammatory cytokines such as IL-17 and TNFα.
source: However, Cx3cr1+ OCLs are induced by inflammatory cytokines such as IL-17 and TNFα and arise in conditions associated with inflammatory bone destruction (Ibáñez et al., 2016; Madel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cx3cr1 is a marker for MN and DC diversity.
source: In line with our observations in OCLs, Cx3cr1 is also a marker for MN and DC diversity (Ginhoux et al., 2009; Varol et al., 2009; Yona et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: BM progenitors can differentiate into immunogenic Cx3cr1low/negMHC-IIhi DCs or Cx3cr1+MHC-IIlow macrophages with high antigen-uptake and a PD-L1-associated immunosuppressive function.
source: Depending on their environment, BM progenitors can differentiate into immunogenic Cx3cr1low/negMHC-IIhi DCs or Cx3cr1+MHC-IIlow macrophages with high antigen-uptake and a PD-L1-associated immunosuppressive function (Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In the gut mucosa, Cx3cr1hi macrophages efficiently take up antigens but induce lower T cell proliferation compared to CD103+Cx3cr1neg DCs.
source: In the gut mucosa, Cx3cr1hi macrophages efficiently take up antigens but induce lower T cell proliferation compared to CD103+Cx3cr1neg DCs (Schulz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The balance between immunosuppressive Cx3cr1hi and inflammatory Cx3cr1low phagocytes in the gut is essential in controlling inflammatory responses in colitis.
source: The balance between immunosuppressive Cx3cr1hi and inflammatory Cx3cr1low phagocytes in the gut is essential in controlling inflammatory responses in colitis (Regoli et al., 2017; Yin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs were more efficient in antigen uptake but less potent in T cell activation than Cx3cr1neg i-OCLs.
source: Accordingly, Cx3cr1+ and Cx3cr1neg i-OCLs exert different immune functions. Cx3cr1+ cells were more efficient in antigen uptake but less potent in T cell activation than Cx3cr1neg i-OCLs.
evidence: This is supported by OVA uptake assays (Figure 5B-C) and T cell proliferation assays (Figure 5G).

claim: Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs decrease T cell proliferation via immunosuppressive molecules such as PD-L1, Galectin-9 and HVEM.
source: In addition, as Cx3cr1hi macrophages, Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs decrease T cell proliferation, notably via immunosuppressive molecules such as PD-L1, Galectin-9 and HVEM.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 6A-B) and anti-PD-1 blocking experiments (Figure 6C).

claim: PD-L1, Galectin-9 and HVEM are major immune checkpoints involved in autoimmune disorders and tumor-induced immune suppression associated with T cell dysfunction, exhaustion, and low activation.
source: These factors are major immune checkpoints involved in autoimmune disorders and tumor-induced immune suppression associated with T cell dysfunction, exhaustion, and low activation (Bjordahl et al., 2013; Cai and Freeman, 2009; Francisco et al., 2009; Tai et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs act as immunosuppressive cells emerging upon inflammatory signals to regulate inflammation.
source: Thus, their high expression in Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs further strengthens the hypothesis that Cx3cr1+ i-OCLs act as immunosuppressive cells emerging upon inflammatory signals to regulate inflammation, which was confirmed in vitro by a functional immunosuppressive assay (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by the immunosuppression assay data (Figure 6E).

claim: Bone destruction in MM is supported by malignant plasma cells that favor OCL differentiation, including from DCs, through high RANK-L, IL-17 and TNFα production.
source: Bone destruction in MM is supported by malignant plasma cells that favor OCL differentiation, including from DCs, through high RANK-L, IL-17 and TNFα production (Mansour et al., 2017; Noonan et al., 2010; Tucci et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In multiple myeloma, OCLs suppress T cell activation via PD-L1, Galectin-9 and HVEM.
